newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Amended Slovak securities law seen damaging market.
newsitem.headline: Amended Slovak securities law seen damaging market.

text.p: A controversial securities law amendment approved by the Slovak government on Tuesday could hurt market transparency and seriously damage rights of minority shareholders, analysts said.

They said that one of the worst parts of the amendment was a major change that majority shareholders of a publicly traded issue are entitled, at will, to cancel trading of the shares on the stock market.

"Regardless of the fact that the law has to be yet passed by parliament, its approval by the government is another negative step that can create even less transparency on the market," Libor Briska a trader at Creditanstalt, told Reuters.
"Furthermore, it is not hard to imagine the possible negative impact on minority shareholders if the majority owner can implement such a change," he added.

The law is expected to be passed, possibly by the end of the year, by the rulng parliamentary majority of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), the ultra-left Workers Party (ZRS) and the far-right Slovak National Party (SNS).
Brokers said the amendment, if rubber-stamped by parliament, effectively gives the majority owner the right to turn the share into a worthless piece of paper.
The amendment does not stipulate how any changes to an issue can be implemented.
Officials at the finance ministry, which presented the amendment to the government, were not immediatelly available for comment.

"As a matter of fact, the amendment will further worsen the already low transparecy on the market, and may even increase the possibilty of manipulating the market," said Dusan Sykora, a trader at ING Barings.

Sykora said the rights of minority shareholders could be protected if the law had a clause stating the cancellation of public trading of an issue had to be approved by a two-thirds majority at a general shareholders meeting.
